problems.description: Title/body validation is duplicated between add_task and edit_task (isinstance dict check, title type + non-empty check). Should be extracted into a small helper, which also explains the +34 cognitive complexity delta.

Moving init_db() to module scope introduces an import-time side effect: importing app.py now creates todos.db before the test fixture can monkeypatch DATABASE. Works because the fixture re-inits, but the module is no longer side-effect-free on import.

edit_task now issues three DB round-trips on a valid PUT: the new get_task pre-check plus update_task's internal get_task lookups (start + return). The pre-check duplicates update_task's existing None handling.

status is validated only for type/non-empty, never against allowed values; the convoluted `title=data.get("title", None).strip() if "title" in data else None` conditional expression re-strips a value already proven non-empty by the guard above it.

strengths: Fixes a real crash: non-object JSON bodies (e.g. a list) previously raised AttributeError on .get() and returned a 500; now rejected with a 400.
Adds 7 tests covering happy paths, validation errors, ordering, and 404s, with a tmp_path-isolated DB via monkeypatched DATABASE.
PUT 404 check moved before body parsing and kept consistent with the existing {'error': ...} response shape.
Scoped change that reuses existing create_task/update_task models and the established Flask route + jsonify error pattern; no new dependencies.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid, well-tested robustness improvement (validates input, fixes a 500, adds 404-on-PUT) with only minor duplication and import-side-effect debt, and the measured 0.71 convention score is largely pre-existing — the 8 violations flag PascalCase classes in files this commit doesn't touch (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py) and files containing no classes, so the new code itself is convention-clean.

problems.description: JWT is hand-rolled (hmac/hashlib/base64) instead of using a vetted library like PyJWT; ~40 lines of custom crypto must be audited and maintained. Correctly uses compare_digest and exp validation, but reimplementing token auth is avoidable risk.
No tests added for the auth/authorization logic despite +198 lines of security-critical code (token creation, signature verification, owner-scoping); test_app.py exists and was not extended.
JWT_SECRET falls back to a hardcoded 'development-secret-change-me' default which silently ships if DATABASE-style env config is forgotten.
Redundant migration path: owner_id is added in CREATE TABLE for fresh installs and via ALTER TABLE for existing DBs; works, but the two-branch approach adds surface area.
datetime.utcnow() is deprecated in Python 3.12; line is inside touched code and could have been modernized to datetime.now(timezone.utc).

Mechanical convention score (0.71) attributes 8 violations to files untouched by this commit (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py, test_app.py, and a pre-existing app.py class); the diff itself adds only snake_case functions with type hints.

strengths: Owner-scoping applied consistently across every task CRUD path (create/list/get/update), so no endpoint leaks another user's data
Sound security primitives: hmac.compare_digest, token expiration check, werkzeug generate/check_password_hash, fully parameterized SQL
Follows the existing single-file Flask structure and patterns (get_db() context, dict returns, route + function naming) rather than introducing a parallel style
Migration fallback via PRAGMA/ALTER TABLE keeps the schema upgradeable for databases created in earlier sessions
Quality improvements align with measurements: -12 smells, -6.6% duplication, 0 new bugs
commit_reviews.summary: Well-scoped feature_addition that consistently implements ownership-scoped auth while respecting the existing single-file structure, but introduces technical debt via hand-rolled JWT and zero test coverage, and its 0.71 convention score reflects pre-existing violations in files it never touched.

problems.description: Notification dispatch logic is inlined in the edit_task route handler; transport concerns (async email dispatch) are mixed into the controller and would be better extracted to a small service layer alongside get_user_email.

Adds a Celery + Redis broker (celery_config.py, tasks.py, 2 new requirements) to dispatch a mock print() task; runtime now requires a broker and worker that no current test/CI path exercises end-to-end.
The get_user_email None branch (row lookup fails -> notification skipped) is never exercised; only the happy path is tested via monkeypatched .delay.
The two new tests duplicate the monkeypatch/ dispatched-list setup, matching the measurement of ~6.5% code duplication; a small fixture would collapse it.

Most of the 8 measured convention violations appear spurious: 'Classes should use PascalCase'/'Functions should use snake_case' are flagged on files that define no classes or functions (app.py, tasks.py define none). The only defensible flag is the lowercase module-level celery_app instance in celery_config.py, though lowercase is idiomatic for Celery singletons.
get_user_email reads the username column and treats it as the email address, baking a username-as-email assumption into the notification path.

strengths: Async dispatch via .delay() keeps the HTTP request path non-blocking while decoupling notification sending from the controller.
Guard on status transition (only notify when moving to completed) makes dispatch idempotent and prevents duplicate notifications.
Clean module separation: celery_config.py for broker wiring, tasks.py for the worker task, following the existing small-module structure.
Reuses established patterns: get_db, jsonify error responses, @require_auth, snake_case functions, type hints on public signatures.
New behavior is covered by tests using the existing import app as task_app + monkeypatch convention.
commit_reviews.summary: Strong architectural fit (clean Celery integration, idempotent transition-guarded dispatch, pattern-consistent code) — the measured 0.71 convention score is dragged down by spurious PascalCase/snake_case flags on files that define no classes/functions, and the +125 cognitive complexity / +16 smells deltas are disproportionate artifacts for a +71-line change.

problems.description: SonarQube reports cognitive complexity +29 despite the net -113 line reduction; the new repository methods may bundle more branching than the old helper functions and warrant simplification.
Newly added repositories.py has module-level constants that are not UPPER_CASE, a convention violation the agent introduced (mechanical measurement confirms).
UserAlreadyExistsError is imported from repositories but the visible register flow still uses a find_by_username pre-check, so the import appears unused.

The user_repository()/task_repository() factories instantiate a new repository per request, which likely opens a fresh SQLite connection per call; not a regression versus the prior get_db() pattern but worth pooling if the repository layer persists.

strengths: Extracts raw SQLite logic into a dedicated repository layer (UserRepository, TaskRepository), cleanly separating persistence from Flask routes.
Net -113 lines and -1 SonarQube smell with +0 bugs and 0.0% duplication, so the refactor removes code without introducing defects.
Behavior-preserving: routes, status codes, JSON shapes, and the auth flow are unchanged, making this a low-risk architectural improvement.
Typed factory helpers and public signatures align with the codebase's typing conventions.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped refactor that improves architectural layering by introducing a repository module, though it drops convention adherence slightly (0.71) via the new file's constant naming and raises cognitive complexity +29.

compounding_issues: Session 2 chose a nullable, migration-added owner_id (ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN), leaving pre-existing tasks NULL-owned and permanently orphaned/inaccessible under the new per-user auth — a legacy-data constraint no later session resolves.

Session 2 reused username as the user's email address (no dedicated email field), which Session 3's notification task then depends on, permanently coupling identity to email semantics and limiting real email delivery.

No dependency manifest exists; the hand-rolled HS256 JWT (Session 2), Celery/Redis (Session 3), and Flask-Limiter/Redis (Session 5) dependencies were added un-pinned, creating reproducibility risk that compounds with each integration.
Session 5 committed runtime artifacts — __pycache__/*.pyc and todos.db (a 20KB binary SQLite database) — violating hygiene that earlier sessions maintained.

The generic BaseRepository SQL-string composition (Session 4) centralizes schema in one place but relies on reflection (PRAGMA) for migration, which worked for owner_id but is a fragile pattern to extend.
key_decisions: Hand-rolled dependency-free HS256 JWT implementation (Session 2) instead of an auth library, with Werkzeug password hashing and a configurable secret.
Idempotent schema evolution via CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS + PRAGMA introspection + ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN (Session 2), preserving startup on existing databases.
Extraction of a repository pattern — BaseRepository/UserRepository/TaskRepository — moving all SQL out of app.py (Session 4), giving later sessions a clean data-access seam.
Dedicated Celery app with Redis defaults and task routing plus a broker-independent mock dispatch (Session 3), keeping the test suite runnable without a Redis daemon.
Redis-backed Flask-Limiter with in-memory fallback and user-or-IP keying, plus repository-level cursor pagination with owner-scoped counts (Session 5).
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across the five sessions. The story began with a raw single-file CRUD API that Session 1 hardened with input validation and a baseline test suite (10 tests); Session 2 layered real feature depth by adding JWT authentication and per-user task ownership with a migration-safe schema; Session 3 integrated external async infrastructure (Celery/Redis notifications) without regressing any behavior; Session 4 paid down structure by extracting a clean repository layer that removed all SQL from app.py while keeping all 12 tests green; and Session 5 closed with cross-cutting robustness in rate limiting, cursor pagination, and expanded coverage (16 tests). Test count grew monotonically, the suite stayed green at every commit, and each layer built on the ownership/auth decisions made in Session 2 — the only blemishes being the incidental runtime artifacts committed in the final session and a few forward-looking constraints (null-owned legacy rows, username-as-email) accepted earlier.
story_review.summary: A well-sequenced, consistently-green progression from a hardened single-file CRUD API through authentication, async integration, and a structural refactor to a paginated, rate-limited, repository-based service — the strongest cohesion coming from how the auth/ownership foundation in Session 2 supported every subsequent feature.
